analogy.p: Think of RAM as your desk: the papers you are working on right now are spread out where you can reach them instantly, but the desk is small and is cleared at the end of the day (volatile). The filing cabinet is secondary storage: large and permanent but you must walk over to get things. The laminated 'how to open the office' instructions fixed on the wall are ROM: always there and never changed. If your desk gets full you put some papers in a box under the desk, which is like virtual memory: they are safe but slower to get back. The analogy breaks down because the box under the desk would still be accessible by you, whereas the CPU can only work on data that has been brought back into RAM.
analogy.t: A desk, a filing cabinet and a notice board

bullets: Know the **need for primary storage**: the CPU can only work directly with data held in primary storage.
Know the **difference between RAM and ROM**, covering volatility, read/write ability, size and contents.
Know the **purpose of ROM**: it holds the **bootstrap** (start-up instructions) so the computer can start.
Know the **purpose of RAM**: it holds the OS, programs and data that are **currently in use**.
Know the **need for virtual memory** and **how it is used** when RAM is full.
Be ready to apply these to scenarios such as a slow computer with too many programs open.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.2 (Memory and storage) starts with primary storage, which is the memory the CPU can reach directly. You must be able to explain the need for primary storage, state the difference between RAM and ROM, describe the purpose of ROM and the purpose of RAM in a computer system, and explain the need for virtual memory and how it is used. These are tested on Paper 1 as short 1 to 2 mark recall questions, 4 mark compare and describe questions, and sometimes as part of a 6 mark discuss question about a computer's performance.

bullets: **Primary storage** = memory that the **CPU can access directly** (RAM and ROM; cache is also fast memory close to the CPU).
The CPU **fetches instructions** from primary storage one at a time using the address bus and data bus.
Primary storage is **much faster** than secondary storage, so it prevents the CPU from waiting around.
Secondary storage is **not directly accessible** by the CPU: data must be **loaded into RAM first**.
Without primary storage the CPU would have **nowhere to read instructions from** and nowhere to put results.
Primary storage is usually **smaller and more expensive per GB** than secondary storage, which is why both are needed.
Link: the speed gap is why **cache** (inside or very near the CPU) exists as well.
core.h: Why a computer needs primary storage
core.p: The CPU carries out the fetch-decode-execute cycle, and every instruction and piece of data it needs must be fetched from memory. The CPU is extremely fast, so it can only keep up if the instructions are held in a place that it can access directly and quickly. Primary storage is exactly that: memory directly accessible by the CPU, connected to it by buses. Secondary storage (hard drives, SSDs, optical discs) is much too slow and is not directly accessed by the CPU, so programs must first be copied into primary storage before they can run.

bullets: RAM = **Random Access Memory**; it is **volatile** (contents **lost when power is off**).
RAM is **read and write**: data can be read, changed and overwritten constantly.
It stores the **operating system, running programs and data currently in use**.
Any location can be reached directly, in roughly the **same time**, which is the meaning of **random access**.
It is **much faster** than secondary storage but **more expensive per GB**, so computers have far less RAM than storage.
If a computer loses power, any **unsaved work in RAM is lost**, which is why you must save to secondary storage.
Typical sizes in modern computers are several gigabytes (for example 8 GB or 16 GB), which will vary by device.
core.p: RAM is the main working memory of the computer. When you open a program or a file, the operating system copies it from secondary storage into RAM, because the CPU can only work with it quickly from there. RAM can be both read from and written to, and the CPU can reach any location in about the same time, which is why it is called random access. RAM is volatile, which means its contents are lost when the power is turned off.

bullets: Step 1: you double click a program; the **OS loads it from secondary storage into RAM**.
Step 2: the CPU **fetches instructions** from RAM using the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Step 3: data you type or create is **held in RAM** while you work.
Step 4: when you press save, the data is **copied from RAM to secondary storage** so it is not lost.
Step 5: when you close the program its space in RAM is **released** for other programs.
**More RAM** means more programs and larger files can be held at once, so the computer is less likely to slow down.
RAM size is **not** the same as storage size: a laptop might have 8 GB of RAM but 512 GB of storage.
core.h: What happens inside RAM when a program is used
core.p: RAM is a temporary workspace that is constantly changing. When a program is opened its instructions are loaded into RAM; when you open a document, its data is loaded too; when you close the program, that space is freed up for something else. The CPU fetches instructions from RAM one at a time, and any results it produces (such as the text you are typing) are written back to RAM until you choose to save them to secondary storage.

bullets: ROM = **Read Only Memory**; it is **non-volatile** (contents **kept when power is off**).
The contents are **read only**: they cannot be changed by the user in normal use.
It stores the **bootstrap** (start-up program) and, in many computers, the **BIOS/firmware** that checks the hardware.
ROM is **much smaller** than RAM, typically holding only a small amount of essential instructions.
Contents are written **at manufacture**, so they are always there when the computer is switched on.
Embedded systems (such as a washing machine) also keep their **fixed program in ROM-type memory**.
ROM is needed because **RAM is empty at start-up** and the CPU needs instructions to start with.
core.p: ROM is memory whose contents are set when it is manufactured and which cannot normally be changed by the user or by normal programs. It is non-volatile, so it keeps its contents when the power is switched off, which is essential for storing the instructions a computer needs the moment it is turned on. ROM is usually very small compared with RAM because it only needs to store a small number of essential instructions.

bullets: Step 1: power is switched on and **RAM is empty**.
Step 2: the CPU runs the **bootstrap program stored in ROM**.
Step 3: the start-up code **checks that essential hardware** is working.
Step 4: it **locates and loads the operating system** from secondary storage into RAM.
Step 5: the **OS takes control** and the computer is ready to use.
This is why ROM must be **non-volatile**: otherwise the start-up instructions would vanish when switched off.
Model sentence: the purpose of ROM is to **store the bootstrap** (start-up instructions) that **start the computer**.
core.h: The purpose of ROM: starting the computer (booting)
core.p: When a computer is switched on, RAM is empty because it is volatile, and the operating system is stored on secondary storage. The CPU therefore needs a small program that it can find automatically and that never disappears. This is the bootstrap, stored in ROM. It tells the computer to check its hardware and then to load the operating system from secondary storage into RAM. Once the operating system is in RAM, it takes over and the user can open programs.

bullets: **Volatility**: RAM is **volatile**; ROM is **non-volatile**.
**Read/write**: RAM can be **read and written**; ROM is **read only** (in normal use).
**Purpose**: RAM holds **programs and data currently in use**; ROM holds **start-up (bootstrap) instructions**.
**Size**: RAM is **large** (gigabytes); ROM is **small** (megabytes or less).
**Contents**: RAM contents **change constantly**; ROM contents are **fixed at manufacture**.
**Power off**: RAM contents are **lost**; ROM contents are **kept**.
Both are **primary storage** and both are directly accessible by the CPU.
core.h: RAM versus ROM: the comparison you must be able to write
core.p: Mark schemes award marks for pairs of contrasting points, so learn the comparison as a table in your head. The key ideas are volatility, whether the contents can be changed, what each is used for, and relative size. Whenever you are asked for a difference, state both sides explicitly rather than only describing one, because 'RAM is volatile' alone does not tell the examiner you know what ROM is.

bullets: The **need**: there is **not enough RAM** to hold everything that is running or open.
Virtual memory lets the computer **carry on working** instead of crashing or refusing to open programs.
It is a **section of secondary storage** (the hard drive or SSD) that is **used as if it were RAM**.
It is cheaper than buying more RAM but is a **slower** solution.
It is managed **automatically by the operating system**; the user does not have to do anything.
Virtual memory exists because **RAM is expensive and limited** while storage is cheaper and larger.
core.p: RAM is limited in size, and modern users often open many programs and large files at once. If the total amount of data needed exceeds the available RAM, the computer cannot hold it all, and without a solution programs would crash or refuse to open. Virtual memory is the solution: part of secondary storage is used as an extension of RAM, so that the computer can keep running even when RAM is full.

bullets: Step 1: **RAM fills up** as more programs and files are opened.
Step 2: the OS **moves data that is not currently needed** from RAM to the **virtual memory** on secondary storage.
Step 3: this **frees space in RAM** for the data being used now.
Step 4: when the moved data is **needed again**, it is **swapped back into RAM** (and other idle data may be swapped out).
Because the data has to be **transferred to and from secondary storage**, which is slower than RAM, the computer becomes **slower**.
The CPU still **only executes from RAM**: virtual memory is a place to store idle data, not to run it.
core.h: Virtual memory: how it is used
core.p: When RAM becomes full, the operating system looks for data that is not currently being used, for example a program that has been minimised in the background. It copies this data from RAM into a reserved area of secondary storage, which is the virtual memory, and this frees space in RAM for the data that is needed right now. If the moved data is needed again, the OS swaps it back into RAM, possibly moving something else out. The CPU can only work with data in RAM, so the swapping is constant while the computer is busy.

bullets: Secondary storage is **slower than RAM**, so reading and writing virtual memory is **slower**.
Heavy use of virtual memory makes the computer **noticeably slow** or makes programs freeze briefly.
Excessive swapping (**thrashing**) means more time is spent **moving data than processing it** (an extension idea).
Virtual memory on a hard drive is slower than on an **SSD**, which has no moving parts.
**Adding more RAM** reduces how often virtual memory is needed and so improves performance.
Closing unused programs also **frees RAM** and reduces swapping.
Virtual memory **wears** flash storage slightly with many writes, so it is a trade-off (extension idea).
core.h: The cost of virtual memory: performance
core.p: Virtual memory is not as fast as real RAM because secondary storage is far slower than RAM, even if it is an SSD. Moving data back and forth takes time, and the CPU may have to wait. If the computer spends most of its time swapping data between RAM and virtual memory instead of doing useful work, performance drops sharply, an effect called thrashing. The best fix is to add more RAM or to close programs that are not needed.

bullets: **Speed (fastest to slowest)**: CPU registers, then cache, then RAM, then secondary storage.
**Size (smallest to largest)**: registers, cache, RAM, then secondary storage.
**Cost per GB (highest to lowest)**: registers and cache, RAM, then secondary storage.
Only **primary storage** is directly accessed by the CPU; **secondary storage is not**.
**Secondary storage** is non-volatile and used for long-term storage of files and the OS.
**Embedded systems** store fixed programs in non-volatile memory, linking to topic 1.1.
**Units** of capacity (bytes, KB, MB, GB, TB) are covered in the next specification point.
core.h: Primary storage and the wider system
core.p: The topics in section 1.1 and 1.2 link together, and OCR often tests the connections. The CPU fetches from RAM using the fetch-decode-execute cycle; cache holds frequently used instructions even closer to the CPU; ROM holds the bootstrap; and secondary storage holds everything permanently. Understanding the order of speed and size helps you explain why computers use a mix of different memory types.

bullets: 'Laptop is slow with many programs open' = **RAM is full**, so the OS uses **virtual memory**, which is **slower** because secondary storage is slow.
'Why can a computer not start with just RAM?' = **RAM is volatile and empty at start-up**, so it needs the **bootstrap in ROM**.
'Why is data lost when the power is cut?' = it was in **RAM, which is volatile**, and had not been saved.
'Why does a computer have both RAM and secondary storage?' = RAM is **fast but volatile and limited**, storage is **slower but permanent and large**.
'Suggest how to improve performance' = **add more RAM** (or close programs), because this reduces use of virtual memory.
'Where is the OS stored?' = on **secondary storage**, and the **copy in use is loaded into RAM**.
core.h: Common exam scenarios and how to answer them
core.p: OCR likes to put these ideas into a context: a user complains that their laptop slows down when many tabs are open, or a manufacturer needs to decide what memory to put in a device. The marks come from identifying the right term and then explaining the consequence. You should always link the cause (RAM full) to the effect (virtual memory used, slower, data swapped) and to a fix (more RAM or closing programs).

bullets: Design trade-off: **fast memory is expensive and volatile**, **cheap memory is slow and permanent**.
A real computer therefore uses a **memory hierarchy** to balance cost, speed and capacity.
ROM is not always unchangeable: modern firmware can be **updated** (for example BIOS updates), but this is not normal use.
**Flash memory** is non-volatile and can be rewritten, so it behaves partly like ROM and partly like RAM (it is used in USB sticks and SSDs).
Primary storage is **internal to the computer**: it is installed on the motherboard rather than plugged in like a USB stick.
Security link: because RAM is volatile, **sensitive data in memory disappears at shutdown** (though it may be recoverable briefly).
Environment link: more RAM is better than relying on virtual memory, which increases storage reads and writes.
core.p: Top-grade answers show an understanding of why things are designed the way they are, rather than just listing facts. RAM exists because the CPU is too fast to work from slow storage; ROM exists because something must be present at the moment of start-up; virtual memory exists because RAM is expensive. If you can explain each of these 'because' links in one sentence, you can answer almost any variant of the question.

exam: **State / Give / Identify** (1 mark): one fact only, such as 'RAM is volatile' or 'ROM stores the bootstrap'. Do not waste time explaining.

**Difference between RAM and ROM** (2 to 4 marks): write paired points, for example 'RAM is volatile whereas ROM is non-volatile' and 'RAM can be written to whereas ROM is read only'. One side alone usually scores nothing.
**Purpose of ROM** (2 marks): 'stores the bootstrap / start-up instructions (1)' and 'that load the operating system into RAM when the computer is switched on (1)'.
**Purpose of RAM** (2 marks): 'stores the OS, programs and data that are currently in use (1)' and 'so the CPU can access them quickly (1)'.
**Explain the need for virtual memory** (2 to 3 marks): RAM is full (1); part of secondary storage is used as RAM (1); so the computer can keep running / more programs can be open (1).
**Describe how virtual memory is used** (3 to 4 marks): data not currently in use is moved from RAM to secondary storage; freeing space in RAM; moved back when needed.
**Why is the computer slow?** (2 to 3 marks): RAM full, so virtual memory is used, and secondary storage is slower than RAM, so data transfer takes longer.
**Suggest how to improve performance** (1 to 2 marks): add more RAM / close unused programs; link it to less need for virtual memory.
**6 mark discuss questions**: use paragraphs that contain a point, an explanation using 'because' and a link to the context; finish with a justified conclusion.
Always use the **exact terms**: 'volatile', 'non-volatile', 'bootstrap', 'virtual memory', 'secondary storage'. Avoid 'memory' alone, which is too vague.
If a question says 'in a computer system', give the answer in terms of the CPU: 'so the CPU can access it directly'.

mistakes.r: RAM is temporary, volatile working memory; files are stored permanently on secondary storage.
mistakes.w: RAM is where files are stored permanently.

mistakes.r: ROM is read only and non-volatile and holds the bootstrap that starts the computer.
mistakes.w: ROM is memory that you can only read, so it is useless.

mistakes.r: Virtual memory is a section of secondary storage used as if it were RAM when RAM is full.
mistakes.w: Virtual memory is extra RAM chips.

mistakes.r: RAM is faster than secondary storage because it is directly accessible by the CPU and built from fast memory; it is usually smaller, not bigger.
mistakes.w: RAM is faster because it is bigger.

mistakes.r: Volatile means the contents are lost when power is turned off.
mistakes.w: Volatile means the data is dangerous or unstable.

mistakes.r: The OS is stored on secondary storage; ROM stores the bootstrap that loads the OS.
Virtual memory lets the computer keep running when RAM is full, but it is slower than RAM.
mistakes.w: Virtual memory makes the computer faster.

mistakes.r: RAM loses its data when the power is off; secondary storage keeps it.
mistakes.w: RAM holds the data when the computer is off.

mistakes.r: The CPU only works with data in primary storage; programs are copied into RAM first.
mistakes.w: The CPU runs programs directly from the hard drive.

summary: OCR J277 1.2 asks you to explain why a computer needs primary storage, to compare RAM and ROM, to state the purpose of each, and to explain the need for and use of virtual memory. These ideas explain how a computer starts up, why it slows down when RAM is full and why data is lost if work is not saved, and they are tested on Paper 1 in questions from 1 to 6 marks.

terms.d: Memory that is directly accessed by the CPU, such as RAM and ROM.
Non-volatile, long-term storage that is not directly accessed by the CPU, such as a hard disk drive or SSD.
Random Access Memory: volatile primary storage that holds the OS, programs and data currently in use and can be read and written.
Read Only Memory: non-volatile primary storage whose contents are set at manufacture and cannot normally be changed.
Memory that loses its contents when the power is turned off.
Memory that keeps its contents when the power is turned off.
The small start-up program stored in ROM that loads the operating system into RAM when the computer is switched on.
The process of starting a computer and loading the operating system into RAM.
A section of secondary storage that is used as an extension of RAM when RAM is full.
Moving data between RAM and virtual memory as it is needed.
Any memory location can be accessed directly, in about the same time, without reading through the others.
Permanent software stored in non-volatile memory that controls the basic functions of a device.
Small, very fast memory close to the CPU that stores frequently used instructions and data.
Software that manages the hardware and software of the computer, including memory.
When a computer spends most of its time swapping data between RAM and virtual memory so performance falls sharply.

worked.ans: RAM is volatile but ROM is non-volatile; RAM can be read and written whereas ROM is read only. (4 marks)
worked.q: Describe two differences between RAM and ROM. [4 marks]
steps: Difference 1 (volatility): RAM is volatile, so loses its contents when the power is off (1), whereas ROM is non-volatile and keeps its contents (1).
Difference 2 (use or editability): RAM can be read from and written to (1), whereas ROM is read only / its contents are fixed (1).
Alternative accepted pairs: RAM stores programs and data in use, ROM stores the bootstrap; RAM is large, ROM is small.

worked.ans: RAM is full so the OS uses part of secondary storage as virtual memory; because secondary storage is slower than RAM, swapping data slows the computer.
worked.q: A user has many programs open and the computer becomes slow. Explain why virtual memory is being used and why it makes the computer slower. [4 marks]
steps: The programs and data being used have filled the RAM (1).
The operating system moves data that is not currently needed from RAM to a section of secondary storage (1).
This frees up RAM so the computer can keep running (1).
Secondary storage is much slower than RAM, so moving data to and from it takes longer and slows the computer (1).

worked.ans: RAM is empty at power-on, so non-volatile ROM stores the bootstrap that loads the OS into RAM.
worked.q: Explain why a computer needs ROM even though it has RAM. [3 marks]
steps: When the computer is switched on RAM is empty because it is volatile (1).
ROM is non-volatile so it still contains the bootstrap / start-up instructions (1).
The bootstrap loads the operating system from secondary storage into RAM so the computer can be used (1).
